text: They had spent twenty years visiting country houses, where the Major had shot in the finest woods and his wife had walked through wet gardens, dressed perfectly for every occasion, but all of that was gone. <break time="0.8s" /> Their small income was not enough to live on, and, having no talent for any trade, they seemed to believe that the only thing left to sell was the very look of their class. <break time="0.8s" /> They were, in short, the real thing, a gentleman and a lady, and I had to admit that in appearance, at least, nothing could have been more genuine than the pair before me. <break time="0.8s" /> Still, a question troubled me as I studied them, for I had found again and again that what a model really is matters far less than what she can be made to seem. <break time="0.8s" /> My regular model, Miss Churm, was only a freckled young woman from the London streets, yet she could represent anything, from a fine lady to a shepherdess, with an ease that seemed almost magical. <break time="0.8s" /> Meeting her in the studio, Missus Monarch could hardly hide her surprise that so ordinary a girl should play a lady, but when I asked her to become a Russian princess, Miss Churm was transformed in a moment. <break time="0.8s" /> It was precisely because she was not a lady that she could seem one, and I began to wonder whether a model who already possessed every quality might, by that very fact, have nothing left to give. <break time="0.8s" /> Nevertheless, having been offered the drawings for a splendid edition of Philip Vincents novels, I agreed to try the Monarchs, since its first book, Rutland Ramsay, was full of gentlemen and ladies.
